input.question: If Germany wasn't a country at the time, how come Martin Luther was considered German? What nationality would he have been considered at the time?
input.ground_truth: Germanic was an ethnic group long before the company of Germany was formed. Germany is really just the latest iteration in a chain of German countries in that area of the world. The Holy Roman Empire was the first "germany", but even before that the Romans would refer to that part of the world as Germania.

Question: If Germany wasn't a country at the time, how come Martin Luther was considered German? What nationality would he have been considered at the time?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a big box of crayons, but some of the colors aren’t named yet. Martin Luther lived a long, long time ago, in a place we now call Germany. But back then, the name “Germany” wasn’t really used the same way we use it now. Instead, there were lots of small groups and kingdoms, kind of like different rooms in a big house.

So, Martin Luther was from one of those rooms (a place called Saxony), and people there spoke a certain language and shared some traditions. We now call that “German,” but back then, people might have just said, “He’s from Saxony” or “He’s a Saxon.” They didn’t say “German” the way we do today.

So, if you ask, “What was Martin Luther?” you could say he was a Saxon, or someone from that area, and spoke the language we now call German. But the country called “Germany” didn’t really exist yet.
